content: The results of the meta-analysis were challenging to interpret due to wide confidence intervals for the pooled effect estimates. No clear impact on cardiovascular or mortality outcomes was observed when saturated fatty acid (SFA) intake was reduced to less than 10% of total energy intake. In a meta-analysis of two trials involving 979 participants, where SFA intake was reduced to less than 9% of total energy intake, no significant effects on cardiovascular outcomes were identified. The Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), which combines serum insulin and glucose levels as a proxy for insulin sensitivity, is frequently used in epidemiological studies. Trials were included in the less than 10% group if the intervention group achieved an SFA intake of less than 10% of total energy intake, while the control group consumed more than 10%. This group also encompassed trials from the less than 9%, less than 8%, and less than 7% groups. Meta-analyses of prospective observational studies comparing SFA intake below 10% to above 10% found an 8% reduction in all-cause mortality risk and a 9% reduction in cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, though the latter was not statistically significant. No associations were observed for other outcomes. Analysis of residuals from regression models for LDL cholesterol suggested a consistent and cumulative relationship between reducing SFA intake and improvements in blood lipid profiles across the range of SFA intakes reported in the trials. This supports the potential benefit of reducing SFA intake to below 10% of total energy intake. The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of consuming less than 10% SFA compared to more than 10% on adult disease and mortality outcomes was rated as low, based on GRADE assessments. For children, the certainty of evidence was rated as high, as results were extrapolated from adult data without downgrading for indirectness. Subgroup analyses revealed that replacing SFA with polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) reduced CVD risk by 21% and coronary heart disease (CHD) risk by 24%, though the latter was not statistically significant. Replacing SFA with PUFAs did not significantly affect all-cause mortality, CVD mortality, CHD mortality, or stroke risk in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Similarly, no significant effects on cardiovascular or mortality outcomes were observed when SFA was replaced with monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), carbohydrates, or protein. However, the evidence for MUFAs was limited to one small trial using olive oil as an intervention, and insufficient information was available on the composition of carbohydrates used as replacements to assess their differential effects. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of prospective observational studies modeling the replacement of SFA with other macronutrients found the following: Replacing SFA with PUFAs was associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality risk, a 10% reduction in CVD risk, and an 11% reduction in CHD risk, though the association with CVD was not statistically significant. Replacing SFA with plant-based MUFAs was associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality risk, a 10% reduction in CVD risk, and a 17% reduction in CHD risk, though the CHD association was not statistically significant. A 16% reduction in all-cause mortality risk was also observed when SFA was replaced with MUFAs from unspecified sources. No associations were observed for MUFAs from animal-based sources. Replacing SFA with carbohydrates from unspecified sources was associated with an 8% reduction in all-cause mortality risk. Replacing SFA with whole grains or low glycemic index foods was associated with a 6% reduction in CHD risk. Conversely, replacing SFA with free sugars or high glycemic index foods was associated with an 8% increase in CHD risk, though this was not statistically significant. Replacing SFA with protein from unspecified or animal sources was associated with a 26% and 31% increase in CHD risk, respectively. No associations were observed for protein from plant sources. Replacing SFA with PUFAs, MUFAs, or carbohydrates lowered total cholesterol levels. PUFAs and MUFAs also reduced triglycerides, the total cholesterol-to-HDL cholesterol ratio, and the LDL cholesterol-to-HDL cholesterol ratio. Replacement with PUFAs had the greatest effect on all outcomes. HDL cholesterol was slightly reduced with all replacements, and a small increase in triglycerides was observed when SFA was replaced with carbohydrates. The certainty of evidence for the effects of replacing SFA with various macronutrients was assessed as moderate for plant-based MUFAs, low for PUFAs, MUFAs from unspecified sources, whole grains, low glycemic index foods, carbohydrates from unspecified sources, and animal-based protein, and very low for free sugars, high glycemic index foods, and protein from unspecified sources. The NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health emphasized that the choice of replacement nutrient is critical to achieving health benefits from reducing SFA intake. Associations between lower SFA intake and improved health outcomes were generally not observed when the replacement nutrients were unspecified, suggesting that some replacement nutrients may increase disease risk and mask the benefits of reducing SFA intake. For children, evidence from adult studies was considered relevant due to the early onset of atherosclerotic changes in childhood, which are associated with abnormal blood lipid levels and other CVD risk factors. Recommendations for children were based on both direct evidence and extrapolated adult data. Tissue measurements of SFA intake, such as plasma phospholipids and red blood cells, were reviewed alongside self-reported dietary intake data. While tissue measurements can reliably indicate dietary intake, self-reported data were more robust and widely available. Individual SFAs, such as lauric acid, myristic acid, palmitic acid, and stearic acid, were assessed for their effects on blood lipids. Lauric, myristic, and palmitic acids significantly raised total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol levels, with myristic acid having the greatest effect. Lauric acid also improved cholesterol ratios, while stearic acid had no significant effects.
